[[File:CSIRO ScienceImage 1319 Food Science Australia.jpg|thumb|Food [[scientist]]s working at a laboratory in Australia]]
'''Food science''' (or '''bromatology'''<ref>{{Cite web |last=Habib |first=Muhammad Tahir |title=What is Bromatology: Definition & Facts |url=https://www.pfno.org/2024/02/what-is-bromatology-definition-facts.html |access-date=2024-10-03 |website=Pakistan Food and Nutrition Organization}}</ref>) is the study of food and its chemical properties.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is Food Science? |url=https://food-science.uark.edu/ |access-date=2026-03-08 |website=Food Science |language=en}}</ref> Its scope overlaps with [[agricultural science]] and [[nutritional science]] and extends to the scientific aspects of [[food safety]] and [[food processing]], informing the development of [[food technology]].

Food science is an interdisciplinary field that integrates concepts from [[chemistry]], [[physics]], [[physiology]], [[microbiology]], and [[biochemistry]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Principles of Food Science|date=21 May 2013|isbn=978-1619604360|last1=Ward|first1=Janet D.|last2=Ward|first2=Larry T.|publisher=Goodheart-Willcox Company, Incorporated }}</ref> It evolved from early preservation practices such as salting to an organized research-driven field central to modern food production.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Processed: Food Science and the Modern Meal |url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/processed-food-science-and-the-modern-meal/ |access-date=2026-02-21 |website=Science History Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> The field includes several subdisciplines such as food chemistry, food technology, and molecular gastronomy, which examine the composition and processes used to produce and preserve food.

'''Food scientists''' develop new products, design processing methods to produce these foods, select packaging materials, conduct [[shelf-life|shelf life]] and sensory evaluation studies of products using [[survey panel]]s or potential consumers, and perform microbiological and chemical testing.<ref name="ift.org Food Science Activity Guides">{{cite web | url=http://www.ift.org/knowledge-center/learn-about-food-science/k12-outreach/activity-guides.aspx | title=Food Science Activity Guides | access-date=February 2, 2015 | website=IFT.org | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150327153718/http://www.ift.org/knowledge-center/learn-about-food-science/k12-outreach/activity-guides.aspx | archive-date=March 27, 2015 | url-status=dead }}</ref> They may study more fundamental phenomena that are directly linked to the production of food products and its properties.

== Definition ==
The [[Institute of Food Technologists]] defines food science as "the discipline in which the engineering, [[biological]], and physical sciences are used to study the [[Nature of food preparation|nature of foods]], the causes of [[Food deteriotration|deterioration]], the principles underlying [[food processing]], and the improvement of foods for the consuming public".<ref name=":1">Heldman, Dennis R. "IFT and the Food Science Profession." ''Food Technology.'' October 2006. p. 11.</ref> The textbook ''Food Science'' defines food science in simpler terms as "the application of sciences and engineering to study the physical, chemical, and biochemical nature of foods and the principles of food processing".<ref>{{cite book| title = Food Science| series = Food science texts series|edition =5th| first1 = Norman N. |last1 = Potter| first2= Joseph H.| last2= Hotchkiss| publisher= Springer| year =1998| isbn= 9780834212657| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=ERoAm13YF8IC&q=Food+science}}</ref>

== Background ==
Food science developed gradually from traditional food preservation practices into a formal scientific discipline during the 19th and 20th centuries. Yet, early food preservation methods such as salting, drying, and [[fermentation]] were used for thousands of years to extend the [[shelf life]] of perishable foods. Archeological evidence revealed that ancient civilizations, including those of [[Egypt]], preserved fish and meat with salt as early as 2000 BCE. Throughout much of human history, the ability to preserve food safely played a crucial role in sustaining communities during times of limited food availibility and war.<ref name=":1" />

==Disciplines==
Some of the subdisciplines of food science are described below.

===Food chemistry===
{{Main|Food chemistry}}
Food chemistry is the study of [[chemical]] processes and interactions of all biological and non-biological components of foods.<ref>John M. de Man.1999. ''Principles of Food Chemistry'' (Food Science Text Series), Springer Science, Third Edition</ref><ref>John M. de Man. 2009. Food process engineering and technology, Academic Press, Elsevier: London and New York, 1st edn.</ref> The biological substances include such items as [[meat]], [[poultry]], [[lettuce]], [[beer]], and [[milk]].
It is similar to [[biochemistry]] in its main components such as [[carbohydrate]]s, [[lipid]]s, and [[protein]], but it also includes areas such as water, [[vitamin]]s, [[Dietary mineral|minerals]], [[enzyme]]s, [[food additive]]s, [[Flavoring|flavor]]s, and [[Food coloring|colors]]. This discipline also encompasses how products change under certain [[food processing]] techniques and ways either to enhance or to prevent them from happening.

====Food physical chemistry====
{{Main|Food physical chemistry}}

Food physical chemistry is the study of both physical and chemical interactions in foods in terms of physical and chemical principles applied to food systems, as well as the application of physicochemical techniques and instrumentation for the study and analysis of foods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Baianu |first=I. C. |date=2011-11-07 |title=Food Physical Chemistry and Biophysical Chemistry |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/npre.2011.6573.1 |journal=Nature Precedings |language=en |pages=1–1 |doi=10.1038/npre.2011.6573.1 |issn=1756-0357|doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Food engineering ===
{{Main|Food engineering}}

Food engineering is the industrial processes used to [[Food manufacture|manufacture food]]. It involves coming up with novel approaches for manufacturing, packaging, delivering, ensuring quality, ensuring safety, and devising techniques to transform raw ingredients into wholesome food options.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Expert |first=E. R. P. |date=2023-03-21 |title=Food Engineering (Goals, Processes, Practices, and Technologies) |url=https://www.erp-information.com/food-engineering |access-date=2023-10-09 |website=www.erp-information.com |language=en-us}}</ref>[[File:Factory Automation Robotics Palettizing Bread.jpg|thumb|A pizza factory in Germany, an example of [[food engineering]]]]

===Food microbiology===
[[File:LUA, Faculty of Food Technology Food microbiology laboratory.jpg|thumbnail|[[Food microbiology]] laboratory at the [[Faculty of Food Technology, Latvia University of Life Sciences and Technologies|Faculty of Food Technology]], [[Latvia University of Life Sciences and Technologies]]]]
{{Main|Food microbiology}}

Food microbiology is the study of the [[microorganism]]s that inhabit, create, or [[Food contaminant|contaminate]] [[food]], including the study of microorganisms causing food spoilage.<ref name=FratamicoBayles>{{cite book | author = Fratamico PM | editor = Bayles DO | title = Foodborne Pathogens: Microbiology and Molecular Biology | publisher = Caister Academic Press | year = 2005 |  isbn = 978-1-904455-00-4}}</ref>  "Good" bacteria, however, such as [[probiotics]], are becoming increasingly important in food science.<ref name=Tannockpro3>{{cite book | editor = Tannock GW | title = Probiotics and Prebiotics: Scientific Aspects | publisher = Caister Academic Press | year = 2005 | isbn =  978-1-904455-01-1}}</ref><ref name= LjunghWadstrom>{{cite book |veditors= Ljungh A, Wadstrom T| year=2009 |title=Lactobacillus Molecular Biology: From Genomics to Probiotics | publisher=Caister Academic Press | isbn= 978-1-904455-41-7}}</ref><ref name= MayoB>{{cite book |author= Mayo, B |editor=van Sinderen, D | year=2010 |title=Bifidobacteria: Genomics and Molecular Aspects | publisher=[[Caister Academic Press]] | isbn= 978-1-904455-68-4}}</ref> In addition, microorganisms are essential for the production of foods such as [[cheese]], [[yogurt]], [[bread]], [[beer]], [[wine]] and, other [[Fermentation in food processing|fermented foods]].

===Food technology===
{{Main|Food technology}}

Food technology is the technological aspect. Early scientific research into food technology concentrated on food preservation. Nicolas Appert's development in 1810 of the canning process was a decisive event. The process was not called canning then and Appert did not really know the principle on which his process worked, but canning has had a major impact on food preservation techniques.

===Foodomics===
{{Main|Foodomics}}

In 2009, Foodomics was defined as "a discipline that studies the Food and Nutrition domains through the application and integration of advanced [[-omics]] technologies to improve consumer's well-being, health, and knowledge".<ref>{{cite journal|last=Cifuentes|first=Alejandro|date=23 October 2009|title=Food analysis and Foodomics |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021967309013545|journal=J. Chromatogr. A|volume=1216|issue=43|page=7109|doi=10.1016/j.chroma.2009.09.018|pmid=19765718|hdl-access=free|hdl=10261/154212}}</ref> Foodomics requires the combination of food chemistry, biological sciences, and data analysis.

Foodomics greatly helps scientists in the area of food science and nutrition to gain better access to data, which is used to analyze the effects of food on human health, etc. It is believed to be another step towards a better understanding of the development and application of technology and food. Moreover, the study of foodomics leads to other omics sub-disciplines, including nutrigenomics which is the integration of the study of nutrition, genes, and omics.

===Molecular gastronomy===
{{Main|Molecular gastronomy}}

Molecular gastronomy is a subdiscipline of food science that seeks to investigate the physical and chemical transformations of ingredients that occur in cooking. The field integrates chemistry, physics, and neuroscience to understand how factors such as ingredient composition, influence flavor perception.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Barham |first=Peter |last2=Skibsted |first2=Leif H. |last3=Bredie |first3=Wender L. P. |last4=Frøst |first4=Michael Bom |last5=Møller |first5=Per |last6=Risbo |first6=Jens |last7=Snitkjaer |first7=Pia |last8=Mortensen |first8=Louise Mørch |date=2010-04-14 |title=Molecular gastronomy: a new emerging scientific discipline |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2855180/ |journal=Chemical Reviews |volume=110 |issue=4 |pages=2313–2365 |doi=10.1021/cr900105w |issn=1520-6890 |pmc=2855180 |pmid=20170128}}</ref>

===Quality control===
{{Main|Quality control}}

Quality control is the process used to ensure that a product or service meets an established set of standards and customer expectations. It involves establishing criteria used for defining quality and identifying problems that affect consistency.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What Is Quality Control? Definition, Importance and Methods |url=https://www.indeed.com/career-advice/career-development/what-is-quality-control |access-date=2026-03-08 |website=Indeed Career Guide |language=en}}</ref>[[File:FoodScience-ex3.png|thumbnail|A technician performing [[quality control]]]]

===Sensory analysis===
{{Main|Sensory analysis}}

Sensory analysis is the study of how consumer's senses perceive food.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ruiz-Capillas |first=Claudia |last2=Herrero |first2=Ana M. |date=2021-03-10 |title=Sensory Analysis and Consumer Research in New Product Development |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8001375/ |journal=Foods (Basel, Switzerland) |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=582 |doi=10.3390/foods10030582  |doi-access=free|issn=2304-8158 |pmc=8001375 |pmid=33802030}}</ref>

===Careers===
The five most common college degrees leading to a career in food science are: Food science/technology (66%), biological sciences (12%), business/marketing (10%), nutrition (9%) and chemistry (8%).<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ift.org/news-and-publications/food-technology-magazine/issues/2020/may/columns/2019-ift-employment-and-salary-survey-facts-and-figures|title=2019 IFT Employment and Salary Survey Facts and Figures - IFT.org}}</ref>

Careers available to food scientists include food technologists, research and development (R&D), quality control, flavor chemistry, laboratory director, food analytical chemist and technical sales.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sfs.wsu.edu/food-science-careers/|title=What kind of careers do Food Scientists have?|publisher=Washington State University|access-date=1 September 2021|archive-date=20 March 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220320055738/https://sfs.wsu.edu/food-science-careers/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The five most common positions for food scientists are food scientist/technologist (19%), product developer (12%), quality assurance/control director (8%), other R&D/scientific/technical (7%), and director of research (5%).<ref name=":0"/>

==Research organizations==

=== Europe ===
{{Main|European Federation of Food Science and Technology}}
The European Federation of Food Science and Technology, or EFFoST, is a European network that brings together professionals working in food science, food engineering, and related disciplines. EFFoST seeks to contribute to the development of safe, nutritious, and sustainable food systems in response to changing global demands. As a regional branch of the International Union of Food Science and Technology (IUFoST), EFFoST partners with over 130 institutions across Europe.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gormley |first=Ronan |last2=Knol |first2=Jeroen |last3=Martín-Belloso |first3=Olga |date=2021-07-01 |title=EFFoST: An information powerhouse on European food science and technology |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0924224421002892 |journal=Trends in Food Science & Technology |volume=113 |pages=430–432 |doi=10.1016/j.tifs.2021.04.029 |issn=0924-2244|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

===Australia===
{{Main|Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation}}

The Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) is the federal government agency for scientific research in [[Australia]]. CSIRO maintains more than 50 sites across Australia and biological control research stations in France and Mexico. It has nearly 6,500 employees.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Policy Commons |url=https://policycommons.net/orgs/commonwealth-scientific-and-industrial-research-organisation-au/}}</ref>

===South Korea===
The Korean Society of Food Science and Technology, or KoSFoST, is a South Korean nonprofit organization that supports academic and professional collaboration in food science. Established in 1968, it serves as a forum for scientists and engineers working in areas related to food production, biotechnology, and product development.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2023 KoSFoST International Symposium and Annual Meeting {{!}} LSTME Busan |url=http://lstme.org/conferences-2/2023-kosfost-international-symposium-and-annual-meeting/ |access-date=2026-02-16 |language=en-US}}</ref> KoSFoST serves as the Korean regional branch of the International Union of Science and Technology.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Australian Institute of Food Science and Technology (AIFST) - International Associations |url=https://www.aifst.asn.au/international-associations#:~:text=International%20Union%20of%20Food%20Science,of%20Food%20Science%20and%20Technology |access-date=2026-03-01 |website=www.aifst.asn.au}}</ref>

===United States===
The Institute of Food Technologists (IFT), headquartered in Chicago, Illinois, is a major U.S. professional society for food science and food technology.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Resources : Department of Food Science : UMass Amherst |url=https://www.umass.edu/food-science/resources |access-date=2026-02-16 |website=www.umass.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Food science is an interdisciplinary field that integrates concepts from [[chemistry]], [[physics]], [[physiology]], [[microbiology]], and [[biochemistry]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Principles of Food Science|date=21 May 2013|isbn=978-1619604360|last1=Ward|first1=Janet D.|last2=Ward|first2=Larry T.|publisher=Goodheart-Willcox Company, Incorporated }}</ref> It evolved from early preservation practices such as salting to an organized research-driven field central to modern food production.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Processed: Food Science and the Modern Meal |url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/processed-food-science-and-the-modern-meal/ |access-date=2026-02-21 |website=Science History Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> The field includes several subdisciplines such as food chemistry, food technology, and molecular gastronomy, which examine the composition and processes used to produce and preserve food.

'''Food scientists''' develop new products, design processing methods to produce these foods, select packaging materials, conduct [[shelf-life|shelf life]] and sensory evaluation studies of products using [[survey panel]]s or potential consumers, and perform microbiological and chemical testing.<ref name="ift.org Food Science Activity Guides">{{cite web | url=http://www.ift.org/knowledge-center/learn-about-food-science/k12-outreach/activity-guides.aspx | title=Food Science Activity Guides | access-date=February 2, 2015 | website=IFT.org | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150327153718/http://www.ift.org/knowledge-center/learn-about-food-science/k12-outreach/activity-guides.aspx | archive-date=March 27, 2015 | url-status=dead }}</ref> They may study more fundamental phenomena that are directly linked to the production of food products and its properties.

== Definition ==
The [[Institute of Food Technologists]] defines food science as "the discipline in which the engineering, [[biological]], and physical sciences are used to study the [[Nature of food preparation|nature of foods]], the causes of [[Food deteriotration|deterioration]], the principles underlying [[food processing]], and the improvement of foods for the consuming public".<ref name=":1">Heldman, Dennis R. "IFT and the Food Science Profession." ''Food Technology.'' October 2006. p. 11.</ref> The textbook ''Food Science'' defines food science in simpler terms as "the application of sciences and engineering to study the physical, chemical, and biochemical nature of foods and the principles of food processing".<ref>{{cite book| title = Food Science| series = Food science texts series|edition =5th| first1 = Norman N. |last1 = Potter| first2= Joseph H.| last2= Hotchkiss| publisher= Springer| year =1998| isbn= 9780834212657| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=ERoAm13YF8IC&q=Food+science}}</ref>

== Background ==
Food science developed gradually from traditional food preservation practices into a formal scientific discipline during the 19th and 20th centuries. Yet, early food preservation methods such as salting, drying, and [[fermentation]] were used for thousands of years to extend the [[shelf life]] of perishable foods. Archeological evidence revealed that ancient civilizations, including those of [[Egypt]], perserved fish and meat with salt as early as 2000 BCE. Throughout much of human history, the ability to preserve food safely played a crucial role in sustaining communities during times of limited food availibility and war.<ref name=":1" />

==Disciplines==
Some of the subdisciplines of food science are described below.

===Food chemistry===
{{Main|Food chemistry}}
Food chemistry is the study of [[chemical]] processes and interactions of all biological and non-biological components of foods.<ref>John M. de Man.1999. ''Principles of Food Chemistry'' (Food Science Text Series), Springer Science, Third Edition</ref><ref>John M. de Man. 2009. Food process engineering and technology, Academic Press, Elsevier: London and New York, 1st edn.</ref> The biological substances include such items as [[meat]], [[poultry]], [[lettuce]], [[beer]], and [[milk]].
It is similar to [[biochemistry]] in its main components such as [[carbohydrate]]s, [[lipid]]s, and [[protein]], but it also includes areas such as water, [[vitamin]]s, [[Dietary mineral|minerals]], [[enzyme]]s, [[food additive]]s, [[Flavoring|flavor]]s, and [[Food coloring|colors]]. This discipline also encompasses how products change under certain [[food processing]] techniques and ways either to enhance or to prevent them from happening.

====Food physical chemistry====
{{Main|Food physical chemistry}}

Food physical chemistry is the study of both physical and chemical interactions in foods in terms of physical and chemical principles applied to food systems, as well as the application of physicochemical techniques and instrumentation for the study and analysis of foods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Baianu |first=I. C. |date=2011-11-07 |title=Food Physical Chemistry and Biophysical Chemistry |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/npre.2011.6573.1 |journal=Nature Precedings |language=en |pages=1–1 |doi=10.1038/npre.2011.6573.1 |issn=1756-0357}}</ref>

=== Food engineering ===
{{Main|Food engineering}}

Food engineering is the industrial processes used to [[Food manufacture|manufacture food]]. It involves coming up with novel approaches for manufacturing, packaging, delivering, ensuring quality, ensuring safety, and devising techniques to transform raw ingredients into wholesome food options.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Expert |first=E. R. P. |date=2023-03-21 |title=Food Engineering (Goals, Processes, Practices, and Technologies) |url=https://www.erp-information.com/food-engineering |access-date=2023-10-09 |website=www.erp-information.com |language=en-us}}</ref>[[File:Factory Automation Robotics Palettizing Bread.jpg|thumb|A pizza factory in Germany, an example of [[food engineering]]]]

{{Main|Food microbiology}}

Food microbiology is the study of the [[microorganism]]s that inhabit, create, or [[Food contaminant|contaminate]] [[food]], including the study of microorganisms causing food spoilage.<ref name=FratamicoBayles>{{cite book | author = Fratamico PM | editor = Bayles DO | title = Foodborne Pathogens: Microbiology and Molecular Biology | publisher = Caister Academic Press | year = 2005 |  isbn = 978-1-904455-00-4}}</ref>  "Good" bacteria, however, such as [[probiotics]], are becoming increasingly important in food science.<ref name=Tannockpro3>{{cite book | editor = Tannock GW | title = Probiotics and Prebiotics: Scientific Aspects | publisher = Caister Academic Press | year = 2005 | isbn =  978-1-904455-01-1}}</ref><ref name= LjunghWadstrom>{{cite book |veditors= Ljungh A, Wadstrom T| year=2009 |title=Lactobacillus Molecular Biology: From Genomics to Probiotics | publisher=Caister Academic Press | isbn= 978-1-904455-41-7}}</ref><ref name= MayoB>{{cite book |author= Mayo, B |editor=van Sinderen, D | year=2010 |title=Bifidobacteria: Genomics and Molecular Aspects | publisher=[[Caister Academic Press]] | isbn= 978-1-904455-68-4}}</ref> In addition, microorganisms are essential for the production of foods such as [[cheese]], [[yogurt]], [[bread]], [[beer]], [[wine]] and, other [[Fermentation in food processing|fermented foods]].

===Food technology===
{{Main|Food technology}}

Food technology is the technological aspect. Early scientific research into food technology concentrated on food preservation. Nicolas Appert's development in 1810 of the canning process was a decisive event. The process was not called canning then and Appert did not really know the principle on which his process worked, but canning has had a major impact on food preservation techniques.

===Foodomics===
{{Main|Foodomics}}

In 2009, Foodomics was defined as "a discipline that studies the Food and Nutrition domains through the application and integration of advanced [[-omics]] technologies to improve consumer's well-being, health, and knowledge".<ref>{{cite journal|last=Cifuentes|first=Alejandro|date=23 October 2009|title=Food analysis and Foodomics |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021967309013545|journal=J. Chromatogr. A|volume=1216|issue=43|page=7109|doi=10.1016/j.chroma.2009.09.018|pmid=19765718|hdl-access=free|hdl=10261/154212}}</ref> Foodomics requires the combination of food chemistry, biological sciences, and data analysis.

Foodomics greatly helps scientists in the area of food science and nutrition to gain better access to data, which is used to analyze the effects of food on human health, etc. It is believed to be another step towards a better understanding of the development and application of technology and food. Moreover, the study of foodomics leads to other omics sub-disciplines, including nutrigenomics which is the integration of the study of nutrition, genes, and omics.

===Molecular gastronomy===
{{Main|Molecular gastronomy}}

Molecular gastronomy is a subdiscipline of food science that seeks to investigate the physical and chemical transformations of ingredients that occur in cooking. The field integrates chemistry, physics, and neuroscience to understand how factors such as ingredient composition, influence flavor perception.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Barham |first=Peter |last2=Skibsted |first2=Leif H. |last3=Bredie |first3=Wender L. ===Quality control===
{{Main|Quality control}}

Quality control is the process used to ensure that a product or service meets an established set of standards and customer expectations. It involves establishing criteria used for defining quality and identifying problems that affect consistency.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What Is Quality Control? Definition, Importance and Methods |url=https://www.indeed.com/career-advice/career-development/what-is-quality-control |access-date=2026-03-08 |website=Indeed Career Guide |language=en}}</ref>[[File:FoodScience-ex3.png|thumbnail|A technician performing [[quality control]]]]

{{Main|Sensory analysis}}

Sensory analysis is the study of how consumer's senses perceive food.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ruiz-Capillas |first=Claudia |last2=Herrero |first2=Ana M. |date=2021-03-10 |title=Sensory Analysis and Consumer Research in New Product Development |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8001375/ |journal=Foods (Basel, Switzerland) |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=582 |doi=10.3390/foods10030582  |doi-access=free|issn=2304-8158 |pmc=8001375 |pmid=33802030}}</ref>

== Background ==
Food science developed gradually from traditional food preservation practices into a formal scientific discipline during the 19th and 20th centuries. Yet, early food preservation methods such as salting, drying, and [[fermentation]] were used for thousands of years to extend the [[shelf life]] of perishable foods. Archeological evidence revealed that ancient civilizations, including those of [[Egypt]], perserved fish and meat with salt as early as 2000 BCE. Throughout much of human history, the ability to preserve food safely played a crucial role in sustaining communities during times of limited food availibility and war.<ref name=":1" />

Food process engineering and technology, Academic Press, Elsevier: London and New York, 1st edn.</ref> The biological substances include such items as [[meat]], [[poultry]], [[lettuce]], [[beer]], and [[milk]].

This discipline also encompasses how products change under certain [[food processing]] techniques and ways either to enhance or to prevent them from happening.

{{Main|Food physical chemistry}}

Food physical chemistry is the study of both physical and chemical interactions in foods in terms of physical and chemical principles applied to food systems, as well as the application of physicochemical techniques and instrumentation for the study and analysis of foods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Baianu |first=I. {{Main|Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation}}

The Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) is the federal government agency for scientific research in [[Australia]]. It has nearly 6,500 employees.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Policy Commons |url=https://policycommons.net/orgs/commonwealth-scientific-and-industrial-research-organisation-au/}}</ref>

The Institute of Food Technologists (IFT), headquartered in Chicago, Illinois, is a major U.S. professional society for food science and food technology.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Resources : Department of Food Science : UMass Amherst |url=https://www.umass.edu/food-science/resources |access-date=2026-02-16 |website=www.umass.edu |language=en}}</ref>

== Background ==
Food science developed gradually from traditional food preservation practices into a formal scientific discipline during the 19th and 20th centuries. == Background ==
Food science developed gradually from traditional food preservation practices into a formal scientific discipline during the 19th and 20th centuries.
